topic: Linear Algebra: The Soul of Matrices (Eigenvectors, Eigenvalues, and Eigenbasis)
target_audience: University STEM students or advanced high school students with a basic understanding of matrices.

outline.topic: Linear Algebra: The Soul of Matrices (Eigenvectors, Eigenvalues, and Eigenbasis)
outline.target_audience: University STEM students or advanced high school students with a basic understanding of matrices.

sections.title: Introduction: The 'Stretchy Cat' Hook
sections.content: Introduce the concept of a linear transformation using a visual metaphor. Most vectors change direction when a matrix is applied, but a special few do not. This sets the stage for defining 'Eigen' (meaning 'own' or 'characteristic').
sections.example: Imagine a 2D picture of a cat on a coordinate plane. If we apply a 'shear' transformation (tilting the cat), most points move to new lines. However, the cat's whiskers along the horizontal axis might stretch but stay on the exact same horizontal line. These whiskers are like eigenvectors.

sections.title: Prerequisite Check: Matrices as Functions
sections.content: Briefly review matrix-vector multiplication (Av = w) as a geometric transformation. Visualize a grid being warped: squares turning into parallelograms. Define 'Linear Transformation' visually.
sections.example: An animation showing a standard grid (i, j) transforming into a skewed grid. A vector (1, 1) is shown moving to a new position (3, 2) after being multiplied by a matrix A.

sections.title: Core Definitions: Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues
sections.content: Formally introduce Av = λv. Explain that an eigenvector (v) is a non-zero vector whose direction remains unchanged by the transformation. The eigenvalue (λ) is the 'scale factor' by which it is stretched, squeezed, or flipped.
sections.example: Graphical representation: A vector 'v' pointing at (1,1). After matrix multiplication, it lands at (2,2). Here, v is the eigenvector and λ = 2 because it simply doubled in length without changing its span.

sections.title: The Math Behind the Magic: Characteristic Equation
sections.content: Explain how to find these values using det(A - λI) = 0. Show that solving for λ gives the 'characteristic' scale factors of the matrix. This connects the geometric intuition to algebraic calculation.
sections.example: Using a simple 2x2 matrix A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]]. Step through the subtraction of λ from the diagonal and finding the determinant to solve the quadratic equation (λ-3)(λ-1)=0.

sections.title: The Power of Eigenbasis
sections.content: Introduce the Eigenbasis: a coordinate system made entirely of eigenvectors. Explain that in this 'custom' coordinate system, the matrix transformation becomes a simple diagonal matrix, making complex operations (like matrix powers) incredibly easy.
sections.example: A 'Change of Perspective' animation. Instead of using the standard X and Y axes, we rotate our view so the axes align with the eigenvectors. In this new view, the transformation looks like a simple independent stretch in two directions.

sections.title: Real-World Application: Bridge Resonance
sections.content: Conclude by showing why this matters. Mention how eigenvalues represent the 'natural frequencies' of a system, such as a bridge or a building.
sections.example: An animation of a bridge. The eigenvectors represent the shape of the bridge's vibration modes, and the eigenvalues represent the frequencies. If wind hits the bridge at an eigenvalue frequency, resonance occurs (like the Tacoma Narrows Bridge).

storyboard.title: Introduction: The 'Stretchy Cat' Hook
lecture_lines: Linear transformations warp space in many ways.
Most vectors change their direction completely.
But some vectors only stretch or shrink.
animations: Initialize a 2D coordinate grid and a simple cat-shaped outline.
Apply a shear transformation matrix to the grid, tilting the cat shape.
Highlight the horizontal whiskers in #FFFF00 to show they stay on the same line.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite Check: Matrices as Functions
lecture_lines: Matrix multiplication transforms vectors into new ones.
Think of it as warping the underlying grid.
A vector moves to a new destination.
animations: Show a unit grid with basis vectors i (#FF0000) and j (#00FF00).
Animate the grid warping into a skewed state using a generic matrix A.
Trace a vector v (#00FFFF) moving to its transformed position w = Av.

storyboard.title: Core Definitions: Eigenvectors and Eigenvalues
lecture_lines: Eigenvectors are special vectors staying on their span.
Their direction remains constant during the transformation.
The eigenvalue measures the amount of scaling.
It shows if the vector stretches or flips.
Formally, A times v equals lambda times v.
animations: Show a vector v (#00FFFF) at (1, 1) and its span as a dashed line.
Transform the plane; show v moving to (2, 2) along its original span.
Overlay a scaled vector λv (#FFFF00) where λ = 2 to show Av = λv.
Display the equation Av = λv in #FFFFFF at the top of the screen.
Pulse the λ (#FFFF00) and label it as the 'Eigenvalue' (scale factor).

storyboard.title: The Math Behind the Magic: Characteristic Equation
lecture_lines: We find eigenvalues using the characteristic equation.
Subtract lambda from the matrix's diagonal entries.
Set the determinant of this matrix to zero.
This creates a polynomial equation to solve.
The roots of this polynomial are our eigenvalues.
animations: Rearrange Av = λv to (A - λI)v = 0 and show it in #FFFFFF.
Transition to the characteristic equation det(A - λI) = 0 in #FFFF00.
Display matrix A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]] and subtract λ from diagonal elements.
Animate the determinant calculation leading to the quadratic (λ-3)(λ-1)=0.
Highlight the roots λ = 1 and λ = 3 in #00FF00 as the eigenvalues.

storyboard.title: The Power of Eigenbasis
lecture_lines: An eigenbasis uses eigenvectors as coordinate axes.
In this view, the transformation is purely diagonal.
Complex operations become simple scalar multiplications.
It makes calculating matrix powers incredibly efficient.
Changing perspective simplifies the entire transformation.
animations: Show a transformation with its two distinct eigenvectors (#00FFFF, #FF00FF).
Rotate the grid so the eigenvectors align with the screen axes (Eigenbasis).
Show the transformation in this basis as simple scaling along the new axes.
Display the diagonal matrix D = [[λ1, 0], [0, λ2]] in #FFFF00.
Show the formula A^n = P D^n P⁻¹ in #FFFFFF to illustrate efficiency.

storyboard.title: Real-World Application: Bridge Resonance
lecture_lines: Eigenvalues represent a system's natural frequencies.
Eigenvectors show the physical shape of vibration.
Avoiding resonance prevents structures from collapsing.
animations: Render a simplified bridge structure using white lines (#FFFFFF).
Animate the structure vibrating in a mode defined by its eigenvector.
Label the vibration frequency as the eigenvalue λ in #FF0000.
